opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd split that into two answers depending on what you mean by "capable."

If you mean a robot that can, in a demo or in a fairly controlled home, pick up the bowls, stack the plates, carry them to the sink, maybe wipe the table, then yes, I think five years is realistic, and in some labs you can already see pieces of that today. The progress in manipulation over the last few years, especially with learning from large amounts of demonstration data, has been much faster than many of us expected.

But a hot-pot meal is actually a really nasty test case, and I kind of love it for that reason. Think about what's on the table afterward: a pot still full of hot, oily broth, little dipping-sauce dishes with sesame paste smeared everywhere, chopsticks scattered in random places, half-eaten food, tissues, maybe a spill of chili oil on the tablecloth. Everything is greasy and slippery. Some things are deformable, some are liquid, some are fragile, some are dangerously hot. And every family's table looks different. For a human that's just a boring chore. For a robot, it's almost every hard problem in manipulation packed into one scene.

So if you ask whether, in five to ten years, an ordinary family could buy a robot, put it in their home, and trust it to clean up after hot pot reliably, every time, without breaking a bowl or dumping broth on the floor, I'm more cautious. My guess is closer to the ten-year end, and even then it might work in maybe ninety-something percent of cases, with a person still stepping in now and then. The last few percent of reliability is where most of the difficulty lies, and that's what decides whether people actually want the thing in their home.

There's also the question of cost and safety. A robot strong and dexterous enough to handle a heavy pot of hot soup has to be very safe around kids and elderly people, and still cheap enough for a household. Those engineering and business problems are not trivial.

So my short answer: the capability will probably show up within five years; the product you'd really trust at your own dinner table is more like ten. And I'd be quite happy to be proven too conservative.

fable-5.1.text:
Clearing a hot-pot table is actually a great benchmark, because it looks mundane but it packs in almost everything that's hard about robotics right now.

Think about what's on that table. You have a pot that's still half full of hot broth, maybe still on a burner. Dozens of small bowls and dipping saucers, some stacked, some with leftover sauce sloshing around. Chopsticks that roll. Napkins stuck to things. Greasy surfaces where a gripper slips. And the whole scene is cluttered and partially occluded, so the robot can't see everything at once and has to reason about what's under what, and what will spill if it picks something up the wrong way.

So the honest answer is that I'd split it into two questions. Can a robot in a lab do a decent version of this within five years? I think yes. We're already seeing systems that can clear simpler tables, load dishwashers, handle deformable things like cloth. The data flywheel is getting faster, and the foundation-model approach to robot policies is improving generalization in a way that would have seemed unrealistic a few years ago.

Can you buy one, put it in a normal apartment with your own weird bowls and your own kitchen layout, and trust it to do this unsupervised, every time, with hot liquid involved? That's the ten-year question, and I'd say it's plausible but far from guaranteed. The gap between a 90 percent success rate and a 99.9 percent success rate is enormous, and for a task with hot broth near people and ceramics, you need to be near the top of that range. The last few percent are usually dominated by rare situations the training data never covered.

The other thing I'd flag is that the hardware matters as much as the intelligence. Current hands are still pretty crude compared to a human hand. Tactile sensing is immature. Picking up a slippery bowl with a thin rim is a different problem from picking up a mug, and most robots today can't feel that they're about to drop something.

So my prediction, if you force me to give one, is something like a lab demo within five years, early products in constrained settings like restaurants shortly after, and a genuinely reliable home version somewhere in the ten-year range, with a decent chance it slips past that. The thing I'm most confident about is that the first versions will be slow and cautious, and that's fine. A robot that clears the table over twenty minutes while you sit on the couch is still a robot that clears the table.

astra-6.text:
I think within five to ten years, yes—but there’s a big difference between demonstrating it once and having it work reliably in your home. After hot pot, you’ve got slippery bowls, leftover broth, utensils piled together, and possibly a pot that’s still hot. The robot has to handle all of that without spilling anything or hurting someone.

My guess is we’ll first see robots that can do part of the cleanup, with a little help from us. You let the pot cool down, and the robot carries dishes to the kitchen and wipes the table. Doing the whole job in any household, at a price people are willing to pay—that’s the harder milestone. I’m optimistic about the capability within that window; I’m less certain about how quickly it becomes an everyday appliance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think within five to ten years, yes, but there’s a big difference between a robot doing it once in a demonstration and doing it reliably in someone’s home. After hot pot, you have bowls, chopsticks, slippery plates, leftover food, and a pot that may still be hot. The robot has to handle all of that safely, even when things aren’t arranged the way it expects.

So I’m optimistic about the capability. The harder question is whether it will be reliable enough, and affordable enough, that you can finish dinner, walk away, and trust it to take care of the table. That’s the standard a household robot has to meet.
